Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

mysterymodel 0.0.0.9000

First development version; nothing is released yet. This records the history by theme rather than by version. Each entry names the pull request that made the change and, where a question had to be settled rather than merely implemented, the record in inst/decisions.md that settled it.

The pipeline

  • mm_full_process(refit = ) and mm_validate(refit = ) take a function(project, draw) returning an mm_model, re-executed inside every resample, so a strategy that selects, tunes or imputes can have the optimism of those choices in its correction instead of excluded from it. It is called once on the development rows first and must give the same equation as the model being corrected; a refit that fits something else is refused there, after one fit rather than after B of them, because an optimism measured on a different strategy is wrong in no visible way.

  • covers and the new held_fixed are computed from the call, and the note is derived from both. They used to be a literal vector and a literal sentence saying “imputation, selection and tuning are not in this pipeline yet”, written when that was true and still printed after mm_splines() and mm_interactions() shipped — so a caller who screened with one of those, picked a term and then validated was told the one thing they most needed to doubt, and test-full-process.R asserted the sentence. held_fixed now names each data-dependent choice the resample inherited instead of re-making (“which predictors are splined”, “which interactions are in the model”) and says that holding it fixed is correct only if it was prespecified.

  • mm_nomogram() refuses to overwrite an exported sheet, and takes id to distinguish two of them. Both fits of a project write <slug>_nomogram.pdf, so the second silently replaced the published sheet of the first with nothing on disk recording which was which. A figure is as destroyable as a table.

  • mm_project(), mm_clean(), mm_eda(), mm_model(), mm_predict(), mm_validate(), mm_nomogram(), mm_interactions(), mm_splines(), mm_calculator() and mm_synthetic_cohort() are the whole public surface. Everything else is internal (#1, #2, #3).

  • The public prefix is mm_ (#4, DEC-002).

  • mm_clean() returns a ledger that reconciles. Rows in must equal rows out plus every exclusion, and a mismatch is an error rather than a note, because a cohort count that cannot be reconciled against the raw export is the commonest reason a published flow diagram does not add up (#2).

  • mm_eda() carries the denominator each percentage is taken over and the missing count beside it, so a percentage computed over the complete rows cannot read as a fact about the cohort (#2).

  • mm_nomogram() reads the drawn nomogram back the way a clinician reads it and refuses to return one that disagrees with mm_predict() (#3).

  • Requires R 4.5 (#15). An exact patch-level dependency is not expressible: R CMD check --as-cran rejects R (>= 4.5.2).

Honest performance reporting

  • mm_validate() returns one row per basis, because apparent, bootstrap-corrected and held-out numbers are not interchangeable and presenting one as another is the commonest way a published model flatters itself (#3).
  • The fixed-model bootstrap is labelled as what rms::validate() does: it refits one formula and does not re-derive anything the formula was chosen by. mm_full_process() refits the whole strategy inside every resample and names what it re-executes (#3).
  • Clustered resampling draws whole patients when the project declares a cluster, including inside rms::validate(), which takes a cluster through predab.resample(). Resampling rows under a clustered design narrows every interval it touches (#9).
  • Resamples that rms could not fit are read off its n column and disclosed. Its own report of the shortfall is behind pr, which defaults off, so a corrected index could be an average over a self-selected subset with nothing on the object to say so (#9).
  • Apparent calibration is withheld rather than printed as 0 and 1. Scoring an unpenalized fit on its own rows forces both, so they describe the estimator and not the model. The identity is detected rather than assumed, so a penalized fit keeps its estimate (#10).
  • One scaled-Brier reference down the whole column, the development cohort’s own, because a column of scores against different references is a comparison a reader will make and should not (#11).
  • The c-statistic comes from the ROC and its bounds from the interval, which are two computations. Reading the estimate out of the middle of ci.auc() discarded a calculable c-statistic whenever DeLong could not be computed (#11).
  • Every interval names its method and the event and non-event counts it rests on, in a new non_events column. An interval that cannot be computed is NA with the reason; one of zero width, which is what DeLong returns on complete separation or complete ties, says so rather than reading as precision; a limit truncated at the edge of the parameter space is named a bound. A corrected c-statistic carries no interval and says why: that needs a nested bootstrap, which is not implemented (#19, DEC-006).

Keeping the documentation honest

  • tools/measure-facts.R measures the countable claims this package’s documentation makes about itself (exports, registered methods, internal functions, source files, test files, blocks, and optionally assertions) and reports whether the README and the validation appendix still state them. It prints and does not fail, because a per-number expectation is one more thing to update whenever a test is added and the pressure under that friction runs one way: the expected number gets edited until the build is green, which is the drift wearing a test.

    It also checks the documents, not just the code, because a probe that only prints correct numbers cannot show that the README contains them. On 2026-11-22 the README claimed eleven exported functions, 318 test blocks, 1301 assertions and 25 files while the appendix claimed 24 files, 271 blocks, 1079 assertions, 10 exports and 15 source files. Every one was wrong, none sat inside a test contract, and nothing failed for weeks.

    Counted phrases that match no measured value are printed with their phrase rather than adjudicated, because a prose count can legitimately be about a subset: “41 blocks across two files” is the saboteur suites, not the suite.

  • review/release-readiness.md corrects its own check row. It had recorded Status: OK from R CMD check --no-manual, which is weaker than the gate: CI runs --as-cran with error_on = "warning", and under that invocation the same tree reported one WARNING and one NOTE. Both are fixed and CI passes, but the row had reported a local run as though it were the gate.

Acting on what validation measures

Ported from the nomogram-final analysis repository this package was extracted from, where each had been written against a real failure. Three capabilities the package measured but could not act on, or did not have:

  • mm_recal_intercept(), mm_recal_slope(), mm_recal_apply(), mm_recal_by(), mm_rubin() and mm_recal_mi() recalibrate a frozen model. mm_validate() reported a calibration intercept and slope and offered no way to correct them, which matters because a reader takes an absolute probability off a nomogram’s bottom axis, so a bias on the log-odds scale is the error that reaches them and discrimination says nothing about it. A correction is monotone, so it cannot reorder any two patients and cannot repair discrimination: that is asserted, not assumed. b is tested against 1 rather than 0, because a slope correction of 1 is no correction. Standard errors are cluster-robust when a cluster is given and sandwich is installed, and the returned cluster_robust flag says which was used rather than leaving a caller to assume. Pooling across imputations goes through Rubin’s rules, because averaging the estimates alone reports the within-imputation error as the whole uncertainty and hides the between-imputation variance, making an interval too narrow precisely because the missing data were handled properly.

  • mm_decision_curve() computes net benefit across treatment thresholds, which the package had no form of. The arithmetic agrees with dcurves::dca() to 1e-12 at every threshold, including ties exactly on the threshold; dcurves is a test-time reference and not a dependency. Computing a decision curve is not the same as being entitled to publish one: net benefit is an explicit trade of a benefit against a harm and means nothing until the decision-maker, the action and the two outcomes being traded are named.

  • mm_vif_check(), mm_redun_check(), mm_cor_pairs() and mm_collinearity_report() are collinearity diagnostics, which the package had none of. Three questions, because each misses what the others catch: variance inflation is per parameter and blind to a variable predictable from a combination of others while correlating strongly with none; redundancy asks exactly that; the Spearman pair matrix names the pair a human can act on. mm_collinearity_report() requires the cohort and checks it against the model’s development fingerprint, because mm_model() does not retain the rows it was fitted on and diagnostics on a different frame of the same shape would read as though they described the fit.

mm_vif_check() gates on the PER-VARIABLE generalized variance inflation factor (Fox and Monette), computed from the correlation matrix of the coefficient estimates, and reports the per-parameter rms::vif() figures beside it, labelled. The distinction is not cosmetic: the bases of one restricted cubic spline are collinear with each other by construction, so on an ordinary model fitted with nonlinear = the per-parameter figures reach 126 and a check that gated on them would refuse every spline model. This is the requirement inst/capability-matrix.md finding 3 had already stated, before any collinearity function existed to meet it. A genuinely duplicated predictor is still refused.

_pkgdown.yml now lists every documented topic, and test-pkgdown-index-complete.R keeps it that way in both directions. The site build had been failing since the accessors were added: a curated reference index is the one artefact that using the package cannot check, so twelve topics had accumulated unlisted, the oldest for weeks.

Outcome coercion in all of these goes through mm_event_indicator(), the rule the rest of the package uses, rather than the private rule the originals carried: a bare as.numeric() turns a No/Yes factor into 1 and 2, and two conventions would let a cohort be fitted one way round and recalibrated the other with nothing saying so. mm_check_positive() refuses a declared event level the outcome does not carry, which mm_project() already does for everything that goes through a project but which these entry points accept directly.

Two functions were deliberately not ported: mm_logit(), a clamped variant no ported function needed here, and mm_recal_axis(), which is bound to the source project’s held-out cycles and artefact layout.

Refusing what cannot be meant

  • A predictor that reproduces the outcome, or its exact complement, is refused by mm_leakage(). Separation that is not duplication is reported instead, because in a small cohort it can be real. A strong but non-deterministic association is not mentioned at all (#13, DEC-004).
  • mm_check_resamples() refuses a fractional, missing, infinite or non-numeric resample count before any seed is set, rather than letting as.integer() turn 2.7 into 2 (#13, DEC-004).
  • mm_metrics() refuses a predicted probability outside [0, 1] rather than clamping it, because a clamped 1.5 becomes a plausible Brier score (#13, DEC-004).
  • Validating against a cohort that is not the one the model was fitted on is an error, checked by a hash of the modelling columns rather than a row count, and a reordering is refused too (#9).
  • A predictor that does not vary among the rows the model can be fitted to is refused by name, with the value it is stuck at. rms reached one inside Design() and stopped with “has <2 category levels”, which gives the variable but not the reason, and says nothing at all for a constant continuous column. Found by running mm_calculator() on the ENT applicant cohort: Step 1 moved from a graded score to pass/fail part-way through the application cycles, so in the development years the field is one value for all but a single applicant, and complete-case selection leaves it constant. The predictor is not useless, it is unusable on that side of the split, and the message says so by reporting how many values it takes across the rows supplied. The same guard names the two all-zero indicator columns in caret::GermanCredit, Purpose.Vacation and Personal.Female.Single, which were previously absorbed into the rank-deficiency message.

Counting the sample that exists

  • Every reported count describes the rows rms fitted, not the rows it was handed. The sample-size gate judged the larger, partly imaginary sample, which made it most lenient exactly where data is most incomplete (#6).
  • Which rows are modelled is decided once, before fitting, and the datadist, the fit and the prediction schema are all built from that frame. Left to na.action the three disagreed, and a value no fitted row carried came back labelled as interpolation while the drawn nomogram reached axis values the model was never estimated on (#7).
  • mm_evaluable() is the one eligibility rule, read by fitting and by both kinds of validation. A missing predictor, a missing outcome and the overlap are counted apart, because taking a missing outcome for a non-event leaves the event count unchanged while inflating the denominator (#8, DEC-003).
  • A factor level carried only by dropped rows is removed and named in lost_levels, since rms answers one with a singular Hessian that identifies neither the variable nor the level (#7).

Patient data

  • The model carries no copy of the cohort. A formula keeps the environment it was built in and rms::lrm() stores that on fit$terms and fit$sformula, so a model built the default way held the whole cohort, patient identifiers included, into anything that saved it. The formula is built in baseenv() (#5). The fitted model went from 176.5 KB to 36.1 KB and 500 planted identifiers to none, with the coefficient fingerprint unchanged.
  • mm_predict() requires newdata, so no patient-level original is retained and no stored copy can drift from the data the caller has (#3).
  • The cost of the empty formula environment is now written down rather than met one package at a time. emmeans, marginaleffects, effects, sjPlot, DynNom and regplot all fail on these fits, for that one reason (DEC-015). rms is unaffected because it reads the stored x, y and datadist. The trade is kept.

The front end

  • mm_calculator() builds a Shiny calculator from model$schema: a dropdown offering the levels the model was developed on and no others, a number defaulting to the median the datadist recorded and stating the development range, and scoring through mm_predict() (DEC-016). Because the inputs and the scoring are read from the one schema the fit recorded, they cannot drift apart, and the startup schema validator that a hand-built calculator needs has nothing to check.
  • The screen carries what the number rests on, not only the number: a gauge whose sweep ends at four times the reference rather than at 100%, the risk as a count out of a hundred figures, the band’s reference printed beside the band, the adequacy verdict with its reason where it cannot be missed, and the coefficient fingerprint. A value outside the development range raises an alert on the face of the page rather than being clamped to the limit, which is what the UTI_Calculator this is modelled on did.
  • Bands are cut on the odds ratio against a reference that defaults to the development cohort’s own event rate, because that is the only threshold a fitted model carries. A decision threshold from a decision curve goes in through threshold. Either way the page names both the reference and the odds ratio.
  • The cut points are odds ratios and not multiples of the probability because multiples stop working as soon as the outcome is common. On the ENT applicant cohort, where 62.4% of applicants matched, twice the reference is not a probability: every applicant above the reference fell into one band and the top two could not be reached at all. A logistic model is linear in the log odds, so a band on the odds ratio is a band on the scale the model works in, and all four bands are populated at a 9% event rate and at a 62% one alike.
  • higher_is says whether a higher prediction is the bad outcome or the good one, and decides which way round the colours and the gauge gradient run. A model predicting a complication and a model predicting a successful match are the same object to the package, and painting a high chance of matching red would be the package guessing. The label stays directional either way.
  • It is built here because nothing in the ecosystem can be trusted with these fits. DynNom refits the model it is handed: adding 0.5 to the age coefficient left its predictions unmoved while rms moved by 9.5, and handing it the whole cohort for a model developed on a temporal split, 404 of 600 rows, moved the linear predictor by 0.130 and the risk by 0.018 with nothing said. regplot has no data argument at all (DEC-016).
  • The nomogram is on the page, below the calculator, and mm_nomogram() is what draws it. That matters more than it looks: the sheet does not appear unless reading it back the way a clinician reads it reproduces mm_predict(), so the figure and the number beside it are checked against each other rather than merely resembling each other. The panel prints the agreement it was granted on, the bound on reading between ticks, and any mutually exclusive axes. A model that cannot be drawn says why in place of the figure.
  • An Hmisc::label() on the cohort now reaches the nomogram’s axes and the calculator’s form alike. rms already carried labels onto a drawn sheet, but mm_model() lost them for factors: droplevels(), factor() and relevel() each drop the attribute a label lives in, so a fully labelled cohort produced a sheet whose continuous axes read as English and whose categorical ones read as column names. The label is preserved across those calls and recorded in the schema, so one predictor cannot be captioned two ways on one page. An unlabelled predictor keeps its column name.
  • mm_nomogram() gained labels, for relabelling a model that is already fitted. The renaming happens after the sheet has been checked against mm_predict() and never before: the check matches axes to predictors by the names the fit gave them, so a caption cannot alter what was verified. Relabelled and plain sheets return identical agreement, profiles checked and reading error.
  • The sheet is sized to the model. Height came from a fixed height = 9 whatever the model, and a nomogram’s rows do not get shorter when there are more of them: the ENT model’s 27 axes on the 9 inches that suited 3 printed row labels across their own tick marks, and the sheet was drawn, verified and unreadable. Height now follows the row count with 9 inches as the floor, and width follows the longest printed name, which shares the left margin with every row’s leftmost tick label. width and height still take a figure when one is wanted, and are reported on the returned object.
  • The risk axis is tick-marked in equal steps of the linear predictor rather than of probability. The sheet is drawn linear in the linear predictor, so equal steps of probability are not equal steps on paper: over the ENT model’s range the default nine ticks from 0.1 to 0.9 landed inside a seventh of the axis and overprinted one another, on the one axis a reader takes the answer off. Ticks are now chosen in the linear predictor, converted, and rounded to figures somebody would write down.
  • The README claimed pagination when a model outgrows one page. There is none and there will not be: a nomogram split across sheets makes a reader carry a running total between them. The page grows instead, and the claim is gone.
  • mm_nomogram() gained funlabel. The printed risk axis was hardcoded to “Predicted risk”, which is the wrong noun on a sheet about a chance of matching handed to the person it is about.
  • audience says who is reading: a "clinician" scoring someone else, or the "self" the row is about, reading their own prediction. They need different instructions. A clinician needs to be told the number is not advice and that the model cannot see the person in front of them; an applicant reading their own chance of matching needs to be told that the model describes people who share their values and not them, that a number is not a verdict, and that it was fitted on people who came before them. The clinical page handed to an applicant warns them about medical advice, which is both wrong and faintly absurd.
  • subject names what one row is. Every sentence on the page uses it, so the ENT model’s calculator says applicant where a clinical one says patient. A page that warns an applicant about medical advice reads as though it were assembled from someone else’s calculator, which is the impression a tool asking to be trusted can least afford.
  • The result column is sticky. With 27 predictors the form is far longer than its own result, and scrolling to the last of them left the prediction off the top of the screen with the right-hand half of the page empty. Bootstrap floats its columns, so the row is a flex container: without that the column is only as tall as its own content and a sticky child has nothing to stay inside.
  • mm_predict() gained interval and level. The limits come from the standard error of the linear predictor at the supplied values, transformed, so the interval is asymmetric on the probability scale and cannot run past 0 or 1. It is computed in a second call rather than by deriving .pred from the linear predictor, because the fitted value is what the rest of the package is checked against, the nomogram to 1e-16 among it, and an interval is not a reason to compute it a different way.
  • The calculator does not show that interval, by owner decision on review finding D-1. It is parameter uncertainty on the probability scale, and a reader shown it beside one person’s risk would reasonably take it for the range that person’s own risk lies in, which is a wider quantity this package does not compute. The number is still computed, still returned by mm_predict(interval = TRUE) and still carried on each saved record; it is the display that was withdrawn, and the panel’s caveat now separates parameter, estimated-risk and prediction uncertainty by name rather than describing the one it used to print. An earlier draft of this entry said the calculator showed the interval, which is no longer true.
  • Rows accumulate and are compared, which is the one idea worth taking from DynNom. A single prediction answers nothing; the question a reader has is what the number would be if one value were different. Kept rows are drawn against a common scale, each row’s estimate marked by a dot and hoverable for the values that produced it, and an extrapolated row says so. No uncertainty range is drawn beside a row, and the axis is scaled by the widest estimate rather than by a bound nothing draws. Drawn as positioned divs: DynNom reaches for ggplot2, plotly and stargazer to put eleven points on one axis, and a calculator that needs no graphics device is one that can be served anywhere.
  • gates couples one input to another: a numeric predictor can be switched off by a categorical one and parked at the value the model was fitted with. A Step 2 CK score means nothing for an applicant who has not sat Step 2, and a form that accepts “not reported” beside a score of 250 submits a combination the model was never fitted on. The control is disabled inside a fieldset rather than removed, so the browser locks it while Shiny still submits the parked figure and the row stays complete; removing it would leave the predictor missing and the row unscorable, which is the opposite of the point. No JavaScript and no new dependency.
  • Not taken from DynNom: sliders for continuous inputs, because a slider bounded to the development range makes extrapolation unreachable and this package allows it and labels it instead; and the model-summary tab, because the adequacy panel and the fingerprint already carry what a reader should act on.

Tests and validation

  • 318 test blocks carrying 1301 assertions across 25 files, including 41 saboteurs verified to fire against deliberately disabled guards (#12, #26), a leakage suite (#13), and a discrimination-interval suite that checks every degenerate case against an independent pROC call rather than a recorded number (#19).
  • Validated against eleven cohorts from outside the package, with every reported number traced to the engine or the hand calculation that owns it. How, against what and to what tolerance is in inst/validation-appendix.md; provenance, licences and checksums are in inst/benchmarks.md.
  • Six defects were found there that the package’s own fixtures could not reach, four of them cases where a default was doing the deciding: a plan inherited through NULL (#26), a factor level chosen by sort order (#26), and a bootstrap seed pinned by design (#26).

Simplification

  • An audit for over-engineering produced thirteen findings; seven were implemented, one partly, and five retained on evidence (#16, #17, #18, DEC-005). pROC was kept because Hmisc::rcorr.cens() returns an interval where DeLong correctly reports that none is estimable, and the capability spike was kept because it still reproduces its matrix exactly. No reported number moved.
